title: Tapping a freshly tutored legend for mana: Relic of Legends versus Esika's granted ability

you: Esika, God of the Tree (entered last turn, untapped)
Relic of Legends (entered last turn, untapped)
Derevi, Empyrial Tactician (entered three turns ago, untapped)
Jodah, the Unifier (put onto the battlefield THIS turn by Sisay's ability, untapped)

stack.object: Relic of Legends — second ability, activated by tapping Jodah, the Unifier
stack.note: recorded here as the action under test; as a mana ability it does not actually use the stack (CR 605.3b)

extras.relic_text: Relic of Legends reads: "{T}: Add one mana of any color." and "Tap an untapped legendary creature you control: Add one mana of any color."
extras.esika_text: Esika, God of the Tree reads in part: "Other legendary creatures you control have vigilance and '{T}: Add one mana of any color.'"
extras.why_it_matters: Sisay puts permanents onto the battlefield mid-turn. Whether those permanents can immediately help pay for the next activation decides whether the deck chains in one turn or across two.

scenario.question: Jodah, the Unifier was put onto the battlefield this turn and has not been under your control since your most recent turn began. (a) May you tap Jodah to pay the cost of Relic of Legends' second ability, "Tap an untapped legendary creature you control"? Cite the rule that governs whether summoning sickness restricts this. (b) May you activate the "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability that Esika grants Jodah? (c) Explain precisely why the answers to (a) and (b) differ, identifying whose ability is being activated in each case. (d) Does Jodah's static ability giving legendary creatures +X/+X apply immediately on entry, and does Esika's grant of vigilance apply to Jodah this turn? (e) How many mana can you produce in total this turn from Relic of Legends, Esika and the legendary creatures listed?

steps.action: Establish Jodah's control history. Jodah, the Unifier was put onto the battlefield this turn by Sisay's activated ability, so it entered under your control this turn and has NOT been under your control continuously since your most recent turn began. Jodah has no haste. Sisay, Esika, Relic of Legends and Derevi have all been under your control since before this turn began.
steps.effect: Jodah is 'summoning sick'. Note the exact scope of rule 302.6: it covers (i) activating an ability OF THAT CREATURE whose activation cost contains the tap or untap symbol, and (ii) attacking. It says nothing about that creature being tapped by any other means.

citations.quote: If an effect instructs a player to put an object onto the battlefield, that object enters the battlefield under that player’s control unless the effect states otherwise.

A creature’s activated ability with the tap symbol or the untap symbol in its activation cost can’t be activated unless the creature has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began.

Informal term for a player’s inability to attack with a creature or to activate its abilities that include the tap symbol or the untap symbol unless the creature has been under that player’s control since the beginning of that player’s most recent turn.

steps.action: (a) Identify whose ability Relic of Legends' second ability is. Relic of Legends is an Artifact, not a creature. Its second ability reads 'Tap an untapped legendary creature you control: Add one mana of any color.' Everything before the colon is that ability's activation cost, paid by you, the player activating Relic's ability. The cost is a written-out instruction to tap a creature; it does not contain the tap symbol {T}, which would instead have meant 'tap Relic itself'.
steps.effect: The object whose ability is being activated is RELIC OF LEGENDS. Rule 302.6 restricts only 'a creature's activated ability with the tap symbol or the untap symbol in its activation cost'. Relic's ability is not a creature's ability, and its cost contains no tap or untap symbol, so 302.6 does not engage and imposes no control-duration requirement on the creature tapped to pay it.

steps.action: (a) Check that the cost is payable with Jodah. Jodah is an untapped legendary creature you control. Paying Relic's cost means carrying out the instruction 'tap an untapped legendary creature you control'; the only requirements on the chosen creature are that it be legendary, controlled by you, and untapped.
steps.effect: ANSWER (a): YES. You may tap Jodah to pay the cost of Relic of Legends' second ability even though Jodah entered the battlefield this turn. That ability is a mana ability - no target, could add mana, not a loyalty ability - so it never uses the stack and resolves immediately, adding one mana of any color. Jodah becomes tapped.

citations.quote: To pay a cost, a player carries out the instructions specified by the spell, ability, or effect that contains that cost.
To tap a permanent, turn it sideways from an upright position. Only untapped permanents can be tapped.

An activated ability is a mana ability if it meets all of the following criteria: it doesn’t require a target (see rule 115.6), it could add mana to a player’s mana pool when it resolves, and it’s not a loyalty ability.
An activated mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated.

steps.action: (b) Identify whose ability the Esika-granted mana ability is. Esika, God of the Tree has the static ability 'Other legendary creatures you control have vigilance and "{T}: Add one mana of any color."' That is an ability-adding effect applied in layer 6; the granted ability becomes an ability OF JODAH, exactly as if it were printed on Jodah.
steps.effect: Jodah now has an activated ability '{T}: Add one mana of any color.' For activation purposes the ability belongs to Jodah - Esika merely grants it. Its activation cost contains the tap symbol, which means 'Tap this permanent', i.e. tap Jodah. Rule 107.5's fourth sentence is scoped identically to rule 302.6 and independently confirms the answer to (b): what is restricted is a CREATURE'S activated ability with the tap symbol in its cost - which is exactly what Esika's grant has made this.

steps.action: (b) Apply the summoning-sickness restriction to that granted ability. It is a creature's (Jodah's) activated ability with the tap symbol in its activation cost, and Jodah has not been under your control continuously since your most recent turn began. Jodah has no haste, so the haste exception does not apply.
steps.effect: ANSWER (b): NO. You may not activate the '{T}: Add one mana of any color' ability Esika grants Jodah this turn. Rule 302.6 forbids the activation, and rule 602.5 means you can't even begin to activate it; if a player nonetheless attempts it, rule 602.2 makes the activation illegal and the game returns to the moment before that ability started to be activated - the entire action is reversed and any payments already made are canceled (733.1). (Sisay and Derevi, under your control since before this turn, MAY activate their Esika-granted copies of that ability.)

steps.action: (c) State the distinction precisely. In (a) the ability being activated is RELIC OF LEGENDS' ability: Relic is the object whose ability it is, you are the activator, and 'tap an untapped legendary creature you control' is merely an instruction you carry out to pay that ability's cost - Jodah is a resource spent, not the object whose ability is being activated. In (b) the ability being activated is JODAH'S ability (granted by Esika but belonging to Jodah), and the tap symbol in its cost means 'tap Jodah'.
steps.effect: ANSWER (c): Rule 302.6 is scoped to 'a creature's activated ability with the tap symbol ... in its activation cost' - a restriction on which of a CREATURE'S OWN abilities may be activated, not a general prohibition on tapping a freshly arrived creature. Case (a) activates an artifact's ability, so 302.6 never engages; case (b) activates the creature's own tap ability, so 302.6 engages and forbids it. Everything turns on which object's ability is being activated and whether the tap symbol appears in that ability's cost - not on which permanent physically ends up tapped.

steps.action: (d) Apply Jodah's static ability. 'Legendary creatures you control get +X/+X, where X is the number of legendary creatures you control' is a static ability generating a continuous effect applied in layer 7c. steps.effect: ANSWER (d) part 1: YES, immediately. On entry you control four legendary creatures (Sisay, Esika, Derevi, Jodah), so X = 4 and every legendary creature you control - Jodah included, since it is itself a legendary creature you control - gets +4/+4 at once. Summoning sickness never restricts static abilities.

steps.effect: ANSWER (d) part 2: YES, Jodah has vigilance immediately - but it is inert this turn. Vigilance only means attacking does not cause Jodah to tap; it does not permit a creature to attack. Rule 302.6's second sentence independently forbids Jodah from attacking this turn, so the vigilance grant changes nothing until your next turn. Vigilance also has no bearing on tapping Jodah for mana.

No creature has toughness 0 or less (every toughness is increased, none reduced); Sisay, Esika, Derevi and Jodah are four differently named legendary permanents, so the legend rule is not violated; nothing else on the listed board meets a state-based action condition.

steps.effect: +1 mana of any color; Relic of Legends becomes tapped. Running total: 1.

steps.action: (e) Tally source 5 - Jodah, routed through Relic of Legends' second ability per steps 2-3, since Jodah's own granted tap ability is unavailable. Sequencing note: Relic's second ability has no tap symbol in its cost, so Relic having already tapped for its first ability does not prevent activating it. STATED ASSUMPTION for this tally: it counts your PRECOMBAT MAIN PHASE ONLY, with no untap effect used. Within such a window nothing is ever untapped, and only untapped permanents can be tapped, so each of these five permanents can be tapped at most once and yields at most one mana. That is a property of the assumed window, not a universal truth about the turn.
steps.effect: +1 mana of any color, tapping Jodah. ANSWER (e), under the stated assumption: 5 mana in the precombat main phase, each of any color you choose - one from Relic of Legends itself, one each from Esika, Sisay and Derevi via tap abilities, and one from Jodah via Relic's 'tap an untapped legendary creature you control' cost. Jodah does contribute mana on the turn it arrives, but only through Relic, never through Esika's grant. Because question (e) asks for the total IN THIS TURN, 5 must be read as a floor rather than the turn's ceiling: any untap effect breaks the one-tap-per-permanent premise above. Step 13 lifts the assumption.

steps.action: (e) Lift step 12's stated assumption. The TURN total is above 5 because this board contains an untapper — but the ceiling is set by how many of your mana sources are TAPPED when Derevi's triggers go on the stack, not by how many creatures attack. The line: in your precombat main phase tap Relic of Legends for its own {T} (1 mana) and tap Jodah to pay Relic's second ability (1 mana), leaving Sisay, Esika and Derevi untapped — declaring an attacker requires the creature to be untapped, so this line requires NOT tapping those three for mana first. Attack with Sisay, Esika and Derevi; Esika grants the other legendary creatures vigilance (step 8), so attacking does not cause them to tap. Jodah cannot be declared as an attacker. The opponent controls no permanents, so nothing blocks and no attacker is dealt any damage; in the combat damage step each attacker assigns and deals damage equal to its power: Sisay 11, Esika 5, Derevi 6 = 22 damage to the opponent.
steps.effect: Combat damage is dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action that does not use the stack, and it takes the opponent from 40 to 18 (22 damage from sources without infect is 22 life lost). Derevi's ability has now triggered three times but has done nothing yet. STATE-BASED ACTIONS: before any player would receive priority in the combat damage step — and therefore before those triggers are put on the stack — the game performs all applicable state-based actions. Nothing qualifies: no player has 0 or less life (opponent 18, you 40); nothing blocked, so no creature has damage marked on it and none has been dealt lethal damage; no creature has toughness 0 or less (every toughness on your board is increased by Jodah, none reduced); and Sisay, Esika, Derevi and Jodah remain four differently named legendary permanents. No state-based action is performed. Your three attackers are still untapped; Relic of Legends and Jodah are the only tapped permanents in the game.

steps.action: Put the three Derevi triggers on the stack — and note that they TARGET, so the choice is made up front, not adaptively. Derevi, Empyrial Tactician reads 'When Derevi enters and whenever a creature you control deals combat damage to a player, you may tap or untap target permanent.' Three creatures you control dealt combat damage to a player simultaneously, so that ability triggered three times. All three are put on the stack together the next time a player would receive priority, in any order you choose; the remainder of that process is identical to casting a spell per rules 601.2c–d, so each trigger's target is announced as it is put on the stack, and a target declared that way can't be changed later. All three targets are therefore locked in BEFORE any of the three resolves.
steps.effect: At the moment those targets are chosen, exactly two permanents in the game are tapped: Relic of Legends and Jodah. Only tapped permanents can be untapped, so at most TWO of the three triggers can be aimed at a mana source that an untap would return to service — target Relic with one and Jodah with another. Pointing two triggers at the same permanent gains nothing: once the first resolves that permanent is untapped, and the second finds nothing to untap. The third trigger still requires a legal target (any permanent is one), but there is no third tapped mana source to aim it at; because the ability says 'you may', you decline its tap-or-untap when it resolves. Resolving the two useful triggers untaps Relic of Legends and Jodah. This is also why the two precombat taps in step 13 are load-bearing rather than wasteful: they are what makes two mana sources tapped, and therefore untappable, at the instant the targets are chosen. THE CEILING IS THE NUMBER OF TAPPED MANA SOURCES AT THAT INSTANT, NOT THE NUMBER OF ATTACKERS — a fourth attacker would supply a fourth trigger and no fourth mana.

The player announces their choice of an appropriate object or player for each target the spell requires.
These targets are declared as part of the process of putting the spell or ability on the stack. The targets can’t be changed except by another spell or ability that explicitly says it can do so.
Only permanents are legal targets for spells and abilities
To untap a permanent, rotate it back to the upright position from a sideways position. Only tapped permanents can be untapped.

steps.action: Decide WHEN to re-tap the two permanents the triggers untapped — derive it, don't assert it. Both triggers resolve during the combat damage step, so the untaps happen there; the open question is whether to tap Relic and Jodah for mana immediately (still in that step) or to bank them for your postcombat main phase. You do have the opportunity to be greedy: the active player receives priority after each trigger resolves, and a player may activate a mana ability whenever they have priority. Count what greed buys: tapping Relic and tapping Jodah to pay Relic's second ability there produces 2 mana; your hand is empty, so there is no spell to cast with it, and the only mana sink on the board is Sisay's activated ability at {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}, which 2 mana cannot pay — a player can't pay a cost without the resources to pay it fully. That 2 mana is then lost when the combat damage step ends, AND Relic and Jodah are tapped again, so the postcombat main phase would yield only Sisay, Esika and Derevi.
steps.effect: Banking is strictly better, and it costs nothing, since nothing in the combat damage step can use the mana. Postcombat main phase: tap Relic for its own {T} (1), tap the now-untapped Jodah to pay Relic's second ability (1 — that cost contains no tap symbol, so Relic already being tapped does not prevent it), and tap Sisay, Esika and Derevi for their {T} mana abilities (3). That is 5 mana in one phase, each of any color, i.e. {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} — exactly one Sisay activation. ANSWER (e) for the turn IN TOTAL: 7 mana produced (2 precombat + 5 postcombat) using only 2 of the 3 combat-damage triggers, plus 22 damage. Honest accounting: with an empty hand the 2 precombat mana has no sink and is lost at end of phase, so the SPENDABLE-TOGETHER total is 5 either way — what the attacking line actually adds over step 12's line is the 22 damage and an untouched, vigilant board, at the price of nothing. Constraints that survive: Jodah still cannot attack this turn, and Jodah still cannot activate its own Esika-granted {T} ability even after being untapped (step 5) — Jodah's mana always routes through Relic's cost. Each further trigger spent untapping a mana source would be worth exactly 1 more mana (Relic via its own {T}, or Jodah via Relic's second ability), but on this board there are only two such sources to untap.

final_state.summary: (a) Yes - tapping Jodah pays a cost of RELIC OF LEGENDS' ability, and rule 302.6 restricts only a creature's OWN activated abilities that have {T} or {Q} in their cost, so summoning sickness is irrelevant there. (b) No - Esika's grant makes '{T}: Add one mana of any color' an ability OF JODAH, and that ability has the tap symbol in its cost, so 302.6 forbids activating it this turn (Jodah has no haste). (c) The difference is purely which object's ability is being activated: an artifact's ability whose cost happens to tap a creature, versus the creature's own tap ability. (d) Jodah's +X/+X static ability applies immediately on entry (X = 4, so every legendary creature you control, Jodah included, gets +4/+4), and Esika's vigilance grant attaches immediately too - but vigilance does not defeat 302.6's separate ban on attacking, so Jodah still cannot attack this turn. (e) STATED ASSUMPTION - counting your precombat main phase with no untap effect used: 5 mana, each of any color: Relic's own {T}, Esika's own {T}, Sisay and Derevi via Esika's granted {T}, and Jodah tapped to pay Relic's second ability. That is exactly {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} - one more Sisay activation, searching for a legendary permanent with mana value less than Sisay's current power of 11. Since (e) asks for the turn IN TOTAL, 5 is a floor and not the ceiling: Esika's vigilance grant lets Sisay, Esika and Derevi attack without tapping, they deal 22 combat damage (opponent 40 -> 18), and each triggers Derevi's 'you may tap or untap TARGET permanent'. Those three triggers all go on the stack together and each one's target is chosen then, before any of them resolves - and at that moment only two permanents are tapped (Relic of Legends and Jodah), so only 2 of the 3 triggers can be aimed at a mana source worth untapping. The best line therefore produces 7 mana on the turn (2 precombat + 5 postcombat) using 2 of the 3 triggers; the ceiling is capped by the number of TAPPED mana sources when the targets are chosen, not by the number of attackers. Jodah still cannot attack, and still cannot use its own granted {T} ability, even after being untapped.

notes: Nothing used the stack in the 5-mana precombat line: every mana ability there resolves immediately (605.3b). Derevi's three combat-damage triggers in the steps 13-15 line DO use the stack, and they target - all three targets are chosen as the triggers are put on the stack, before any resolves (603.3, 603.3b, 603.3d, 115.1).

No state-based action is performed anywhere in this scenario, but the check is made twice: at step 9 (after Jodah's arrival) and at step 13 (after 22 combat damage, before the triggers go on the stack). The legend rule (704.5j) is never violated - the four legendary permanents all have different names - and with no blockers nothing is dealt lethal damage (704.5g).

Unspent mana is lost at the end of the step or phase (106.4), so mana must be spent in the phase that produced it - that is what stops you banking precombat mana for a postcombat Sisay activation, and it is why taking the untaps greedily during the combat damage step is strictly worse: 2 mana there cannot pay Sisay's five-colour cost (118.3) and your hand is empty, so it would simply be lost.

Deck lesson: a permanent Sisay puts onto the battlefield mid-turn can still pay for the NEXT activation, but only through cost-side taps like Relic of Legends - never through a {T} ability the creature itself has or is granted.

Deck lesson 2: with Esika's vigilance grant and Derevi on board, tapping out precombat is often wrong - attacking first keeps the vigilant legends untapped AND generates untap triggers. But size the plan by how many mana sources will be TAPPED when those triggers hit the stack, because that number, not the attacker count, is what the triggers can convert into mana.

findings.note: [status normalised from 'partial' to the contract vocabulary {supported, unsupported, irrelevant, misquoted}] The step justifies all three attackers staying untapped by Esika's grant, but that grant reads 'OTHER legendary creatures you control have vigilance' and cannot reach Esika. Esika stays untapped because Vigilance is PRINTED on its front face, a fact the artifact never states or cites. Outcome right, stated reason does not cover Esika - and step 14's 'exactly two permanents are tapped' depends on it.

LOAD-BEARING DEFECT. 'Only tapped permanents can be untapped' is true but is used to derive 'pointing two triggers at the same permanent gains nothing'. That ignores the priority window between resolutions: per 117.3b (cited by this artifact in step 15) the active player receives priority after each trigger resolves and per 605.3a may activate a mana ability then. Trigger A untaps Relic, you tap Relic for its own {T} (+1 mana), trigger B then finds Relic tapped and untaps it again. A second trigger aimed at Relic is worth a full extra mana. Step 14's conclusion is refuted by step 15's own citations.

CEILING RECHARACTERISATION IS WRONG. 'The ceiling is the number of tapped mana sources at that instant, not the number of attackers' and 'a fourth attacker would supply a fourth trigger and no fourth mana' both fail for the reason above. Because a permanent can be re-tapped in the priority window between trigger resolutions, each additional trigger aimed at Relic or Jodah converts to exactly one more mana. The binding cap on this board is the NUMBER OF TRIGGERS (3), not the number of tapped sources (2). The revision traded one wrong ceiling for another.

[status normalised from 'partial' to the contract vocabulary {supported, unsupported, irrelevant, misquoted}] The honest-accounting concession is correct as far as it goes: with an empty hand the 2 precombat mana has no sink and is lost at end of phase, the maximum spendable-together in any one phase is 5 either way, and what the attacking line adds is 22 damage plus an untapped vigilant board. Independently confirmed. But 'banking is strictly better' and 'ANSWER (e) for the turn IN TOTAL: 7 mana produced' hold only under the mistaken 2-of-3-triggers premise. With the third trigger also aimed at Relic the production total is 8. The third trigger costs nothing to use, so declining it is not forced. The 5-mana spendable figure and the Sisay activation conclusion survive unchanged.

Answer (b): Esika's granted '{T}: Add one mana of any color' is Jodah's own ability and 302.6 forbids activating it this turn.
Answer (c): the distinction turns on which object's ability is activated, not which permanent ends up tapped.
Answer (d): Jodah's +X/+X applies immediately on entry (X=4); Esika's vigilance grant attaches immediately but is inert because 302.6 independently bars attacking.
